title: Fonts with next/font
summary: Next.js font tools help load fonts while reducing layout shifts.

subtopics.title: Choose a source
subtopics.explanation: Choose local or hosted font files deliberately. Local files can provide control and avoid a third-party request; hosted services may offer a broad library. Review licensing, privacy, and loading behavior. Consider the user’s connection as well as the brand when selecting a source. Local and hosted sources have different licensing, privacy, caching, and deployment considerations. Choose a source the team can legally and reliably serve. A font source is like choosing between supplies kept in-house and a delivery service.

subtopics.title: Fallback fonts
subtopics.explanation: A fallback stack gives the browser another font if the preferred one cannot load. Choose a fallback with similar proportions so text remains readable and layout changes are smaller. For example, set a system sans-serif fallback after the preferred family. Test the fallback state, not only the final font. Fallback fonts should support the page’s language and special characters. Compare their widths with the preferred font to limit content shifts. A fallback font is like a backup speaker who can still deliver the message.

subtopics.title: Loading behavior
subtopics.explanation: Font display behavior controls what users see while a font downloads. Showing fallback text immediately keeps content available; hiding text can make the page appear blank. Test on a slow connection and watch for layout shifts when the custom font replaces the fallback. Readable text should appear while a font loads. Measure layout shift and test on a slow connection, rather than judging only the final screenshot. Showing fallback text is like putting up a temporary sign while the final one is printed.

subtopics.title: Use needed weights
subtopics.explanation: Include only the font weights and character subsets the design needs. Extra files increase downloads. For example, if the page uses regular and bold only, avoid loading several unused weights. Check that each file actually provides the requested weight instead of relying on synthetic bold. Variable font files can provide several weights in one file, but still have a size cost. Include only the ranges and subsets the design uses. Loading only used weights is like packing only the tools needed for the job.

subtopics.title: Check wrapping
subtopics.explanation: Changing a font changes letter widths and line breaks. Review headings, buttons, and long labels after loading it. Test translated strings and narrow screens, where wrapping can change the layout. Keep the content usable while the preferred font is still loading. Check text wrapping, controls, and headings with both the preferred and fallback fonts. Font metrics affect layout, especially on narrow screens. A font change is like changing the width of letters on a sign; the words may no longer fit.

foundations.overview: Fonts affect readability, brand, and page loading. Next.js can work with local or hosted font files, while CSS font stacks provide fallbacks. Think of a font choice like a voice: it should fit the message and remain understandable if the preferred option is unavailable. Load only needed files and weights, then check text wrapping and layout.
foundations.whyItMatters: Font choices affect brand, reading comfort, performance, and layout shifts. A considered fallback and limited font payload improve both experience and reliability.
foundations.mentalModel: Fonts affect readability, brand, and page loading.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser downloads the font from your own origin (no fonts.googleapis.com hop), paints text immediately using a size-adjusted fallback, then swaps to the real font with no visible jump because the fallback already occupied the right space.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Almost every Next.js app sets a primary font in the root layout via next/font/google, and brand-heavy sites add a licensed font through next/font/local. Multi-font designs expose each as a CSS variable.
foundations.businessImpact: Lower CLS and faster text paint improve Core Web Vitals, which affect SEO ranking and conversion. Removing Google's font CDN also helps GDPR/privacy compliance by avoiding sending user IPs to a third party.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Developers stop hand-writing @font-face rules, preconnect hints, and font-display hacks. The font is declared once and inherited, reducing styling bugs and boilerplate.
foundations.performanceImpact: Self-hosting cuts a DNS/connection to a third party; subsetting shrinks the font payload; size-adjust fallbacks eliminate CLS; and fonts are preloaded only on routes that use them.
commonUseCases: Setting a single app-wide font in the root layout
Shipping a licensed/brand font via next/font/local
Exposing multiple fonts as CSS variables for headings vs body
Reducing CLS and Core Web Vitals failures caused by web fonts
Load a brand typeface while retaining readable fallback text.
Reduce layout shifts caused by different font metrics.
Limit downloaded font files on a content-heavy page.

commonMisconceptions.myth: next/font fetches fonts from Google at runtime.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Fonts are downloaded at BUILD time and self-hosted on your domain; the browser never contacts Google's CDN.

commonMisconceptions.myth: You must manually add font-display and preconnect to avoid layout shift.
commonMisconceptions.reality: next/font generates a metric-matched fallback (size-adjust) and handles preloading automatically, so you don't write that boilerplate.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A custom font improves readability by itself.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Legibility depends on size, spacing, contrast, language support, and the font design.

commonMisconceptions.myth: A fallback stack means users will see exactly the same layout.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Different font metrics change wrapping, so test fallback and loaded states.

visualExplorer.title: How next/font self-hosts a font
visualExplorer.caption: Follow a font from import to a shift-free render on your own domain.

config.intro: Trace what next/font does at build time and what the browser does at runtime.

steps.name: Declare
steps.detail: You import the font as a function and pass options (subsets, display, weight/variable). This is a build-time declaration, not a runtime fetch.

steps.name: Download & subset
steps.detail: At build, Next downloads the font files from Google (or reads your local files) and subsets them to only the glyphs you requested.

steps.name: Self-host
steps.detail: The optimized files are emitted as your app's static assets, so they're served from your origin/CDN — never from a third party at runtime.

steps.name: Generate @font-face
steps.detail: Next writes @font-face rules including size-adjust/ascent-override so a system fallback matches the real font's metrics.

steps.name: Apply
steps.detail: You add the returned className (or CSS variable) to an element; everything inside inherits the font.

steps.name: Render
steps.detail: The browser paints text with the matched fallback instantly, then swaps to the real font with zero layout shift.

interactiveExamples.title: Simulating zero layout shift (runnable)
interactiveExamples.explanation: A custom font often loads after paint, causing text to jump. This demo simulates the difference between a fallback whose metrics match (no shift) and one that doesn't (visible shift) — which is exactly what next/font's size-adjust fixes.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: After ~800ms the line-height changes to mimic a mismatched-then-loaded font; next/font prevents this jump.

codeLab.title: Apply two fonts via CSS variables
codeLab.instructions: Fill in the illustrative layout so a heading font and a body font are each exposed as CSS variables (--font-heading, --font-body). Edit the `lines` array to complete the two font declarations and the variable classes, then Run.
codeLab.expectedOutput: Two fonts declared with CSS variables and applied to the html element.
hints: Each font function accepts a `variable` option like '--font-body'.
Apply the `.variable` class (not `.className`) when using CSS variables, and reference the variable in CSS.

keyTakeaways: Choose local or hosted font files deliberately.
A fallback stack gives the browser another font if the preferred one cannot load.
Font display behavior controls what users see while a font downloads.
Include only the font weights and character subsets the design needs.
Changing a font changes letter widths and line breaks.
